cards.def: Medieval thinkers divided society into nobility, church and laborers, but by the late fourteenth century the prosperous middle class, into which Chaucer was born, no longer fit these three estates.

Because Chaucer, a wine merchant's son, worked as page, soldier, diplomat and customs controller, he moved among bourgeois and aristocratic worlds, so his poetry juxtaposes their many idioms and voices.
Chaucer began under French influence, the Italian missions gave him Dante's, Petrarch's and Boccaccio's models such as iambic pentameter, but writing in English is what made his lasting fame.

Pilgrims riding toward Becket's shrine may have suggested Chaucer's frame narrative, and unlike Gower's single speaker or Boccaccio's ten elite narrators, his pilgrim tellers span a wide spectrum of ranks.
Because tales are matched to tellers and joined by quarreling links, each tale reveals its pilgrim, so Chaucer runs two fictions together, though his plan of about 120 tales stayed unfinished.
When April showers and Nature stir hearts, folk long to go on pilgrimages, so twenty-nine pilgrims gather at the Tabard in Southwark and the narrator describes each one's condition, degree and array.
Starting with the Knight and running down the lower orders, the portraits form a microcosm of society drawn from estates satire, where clothes, food and work reveal rank and moral condition.
The ideal Knight, Parson and Plowman, who practice what they preach, show up the worldly Prioress, the hunting Monk, the flattering Friar and the Pardoner with his phony relics.
Because the naive narrator suppresses overt moral judgment and even agrees with the Monk ("And I said his opinion was good," line 183), readers must draw out the irony themselves.
To keep the ride merry, Harry Bailly proposes two tales each way with a free supper for the tale of "best sentence and most solace," becomes judge, and the Knight draws the cut.
The Wife opens the next part by claiming her own "experience," even without "authority," is enough to speak of woe in marriage, since she has wed five husbands since age twelve.
Against the idea that one marriage is enough, the Wife argues that God bade us "wax and multiply," Paul only counseled virginity, and wives are barley bread beside virgins' wheat.
When the Pardoner says her preaching makes him dread marriage, the Wife promises tales of marital tribulation in which she herself "hath been the whip."
Because her three good husbands were rich and old and gave her their land, the Wife ruled them by falsely accusing them of drunken complaints and withholding sex until paid.
Unlike the old three, her fourth husband was a reveler with a paramour, so the Wife flirted until jealousy made her "his purgatory," and he died as she returned from Jerusalem.
At the fourth husband's funeral the forty-year-old Wife fell for twenty-year-old Jankin, whom she had already courted with a false dream, and married him for love, giving him all her land.
Because Jankin nightly read her antifeminist tales, the Wife tore out three leaves and he struck her deaf, but in remorse he burned the book and gave her "all the sovereinetee."
When the Friar mocks her "long preamble," he and the Summoner threaten tales against each other until the Host restores peace and lets the Wife begin her tale.
In Arthur's days, a knight who rapes a maiden is spared by the queen if he learns in a twelvemonth and a day what women most desire, which an old wife teaches him for his pledge.
The knight tells the court that women desire "sovereignty" over husbands, which saves his life, but the old wife then claims his pledge and forces him to marry her.
When the knight scorns her as loathly, old and low-born, the old wife argues that gentilesse comes from virtuous deeds and God's grace, not ancestry, and that poverty and age bring no shame.
Offered a foul, faithful wife or a fair, risky one, the knight leaves the choice to her "wise governaunce," so having won maistry she becomes both fair and good and obeys him.
